extracted.intended_audience: researchers, NIH stakeholders, grant reviewers, and policymakers interested in peer review and research funding
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of the predictive validity of NIH peer-review percentile scores for R01 grant productivity, using publication and citation outcomes from funded grants (percentiles ≤20). Focuses on whether peer review stratifies meritorious applications according to subsequent productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile score (NIH peer review ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentile scores awarded by peer review panels (rounded to the nearest whole number); lower percentile scores are more favorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the primary ranking metric in NIH review; analysis shows only a modest correlation with productivity in the top 20 percentiles (slope = −0.132 publications and −9.6 citations per percentile increment, r^2 = 0.0078). Percentile scores explain ~1% of variance in productivity; an outstanding percentile score is not a guarantor of success (17% of grants with score 0 had no citations). Note: fewer grants received a percentile score of zero due to rounding and a change in the percentiling algorithm since 2009.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication productivity (count of publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of publications acknowledging grant support within five years of grant approval (from PubMed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Median publications per grant was 6; publication counts show a wide range at any given percentile score and do not significantly differ between many adjacent percentile cohorts in the 3–20 range. Used to divide grants into top/bottom halves (top half ≥6 publications) for stratified analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation productivity (count of citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of citations received by the publications acknowledging the grant (data from Web of Science) through the end of 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an outcome measure of grant productivity; top half on citation productivity had ≥128 citations. Citation counts vary with cohort/fiscal year and citation practices have changed over time (citations per paper approximately doubled between 1980 and 2004), which complicates interpretation. Limitations of retrospective citation measures as validation metrics are acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity (correlation, slope, r²)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical measures of how well percentile scores predict productivity (e.g., slope per percentile increment, r² values).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The re-analysis reports a modest correlation across top 20 percentiles: slope = −0.132 ± 0.005 publications and −9.6 ± 0.337 citations per percentile increment, with r² = 0.0078, indicating very weak predictive power. These parametric metrics are used to argue that peer review poorly discriminates among meritorious applications in the relevant payline range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminatory ability measured by ROC / AUC
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiver operating characteristic curve and area under the curve (AUC) assessing percentile score's ability to distinguish high vs low productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For grants with percentile scores ≤20, AUC = 0.54 (95% CI: 0.53–0.54), indicating performance only slightly above random chance (0.5). ROC/AUC used to quantify the usefulness of percentiles as a classifier for productivity above the median.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-parametric model importance (random forest variance explained)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a random forest model to measure how much variance in productivity can be accounted for by percentile score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random forest model with 500 trees indicated that ~0.98% of variance in productivity could be accounted for by percentile ranking, suggesting minimal impact of percentile ranking relative to random ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to discriminate extreme flaws vs. fine-grained ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review's capacity to separate clearly unsound applications from sound ones versus its ability to stratify among meritorious applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is general agreement that peer review can identify proposals with serious flaws, but it is uncertain and likely limited in predicting which among meritorious applications will be most productive—especially within the 3–20 percentile range relevant to current paylines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of reviewers / statistical precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequacy of the number of reviewers to provide statistical precision in scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior work indicates the number of reviewers is typically inadequate, reducing precision and increasing chance variation in scores; small reviewer panels contribute to imprecision in ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-reviewer variability and disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of variation and disagreement among reviewers regarding scores and review criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerable variation among scores and disagreement about criteria have been documented; high variability reduces reliability of percentiles as predictors of productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias affecting funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic biases among reviewers that influence scores and funding outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Bayesian hierarchical model found evidence that reviewer bias influenced up to ~25% of funding decisions, indicating that bias is a substantial factor altering which applications are funded independent of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of payline (funding cutoff) to evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Focusing evaluation on the percentile range that is relevant to actual funding decisions (e.g., ≤20th percentile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because NIH paylines seldom exceed the 20th percentile and often are near the 10th, analyses restricted to percentiles ≤20 are most policy-relevant; correlations observed across a wider historical range (>40th percentile) may not apply to current funding contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohort / fiscal year effects on citation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal trends (year of award) and changing citation practices that influence citation counts independently of application quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations per paper have increased over time, and more recent grants may both have higher citation counts and more favorable percentile scores (due to declining paylines), producing spurious correlations; analyses should account for cohort effects where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding exceptions and budgetary impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of funding applications scoring worse than the payline later in the fiscal year and the associated budget reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions (e.g., 13% of R01s in FY2003–2007) often are funded later and may face reduced budgets, which can adversely affect productivity and confound the relationship between score and outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of using retrospective publication/citation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveats about interpreting publications and citations as measures of grant productivity or proof of peer review accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective bibliometric measures have acknowledged limitations (lag times, field/citation practice differences, cohort effects) and thus imperfectly validate peer-review predictive ability; such limitations should temper conclusions drawn from citation-based analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and measurement window for productivity metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational choices for measuring productivity: publications within five years and citations through a fixed cutoff (2013) using specific data sources (PubMed, Web of Science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study used a 5-year publication window and citations through 2013; these methodological choices affect measured productivity and comparability across grants from different years and fields and should be explicitly reported and justified in any similar evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential procedural alternative: modified lottery within top-tier
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal that reviewers identify the top ~20% of meritorious applications and funding be allocated by lottery or programmatic priorities within that set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on poor stratification power within the payline-relevant range, the authors suggest a modified lottery could save reviewer effort and might better allocate limited funds; cites New Zealand Explorer Grants as an example of lottery use.
